title: Indian Chefs Are Taking Regional Cuisine Beyond Butter Chicken to Global Tables
excerpt: From Michelin-starred South Indian restaurants in New York to Kerala cuisine in midtown Manhattan, a new generation of chefs and India's government are working to redefine the country's culinary identity abroad.
body:
• India's government is crafting a plan to position regional cuisines as a global brand, with participation in major food festivals including Taste of London and the Dubai Food Festival
  • Semma, a Michelin-starred South Indian restaurant in New York, topped The New York Times's 2025 list of the city's 100 best restaurants — a first for any Indian restaurant
  • India's ready-to-eat and ready-to-cook food exports grew to $1.69 billion in 2024-25, with the US, UK, UAE, and Canada among top destinations
  • Diaspora chefs worldwide are moving beyond butter chicken and tikka masala to showcase Kerala, Chettinad, Gujarati, and Northeastern cuisines

Beyond the Butter Chicken Stereotype

For decades, Indian cuisine abroad has been reduced to a handful of dishes — butter chicken, tikka masala, naan. Now, a confluence of government strategy, diaspora entrepreneurship, and a new generation of trained chefs is reshaping how the world experiences Indian food.

India's food processing industries ministry is developing an ambitious plan to turn the country's vast regional cuisines into a coherent global brand. The strategy draws on lessons from Italy's success with pizza and pasta, Korea's global push for Korean cuisine, and Japan's washoku branding campaign.

The plan involves identifying popular regional dishes that can be adapted into ready-to-eat and ready-to-cook formats for international markets. Southern specialties like Chettinad chicken, Hyderabadi haleem, Malabar biryani, and Mangalorean ghee roast sit alongside northern dishes like rogan josh, yakhni pulao, and Awadhi biryani on the target list.

Diaspora Chefs Leading the Charge

While the government plan is still at a conceptual stage, diaspora chefs are already doing the work. In New York, Chatti — a Kerala restaurant in midtown Manhattan — serves kappa and red fish curry, sardine fry, appams, and duck curry without diluting the original recipes.

"Indian cuisines have so many hidden treasures to show the world. We serve kappa and red fish curry, sardine fry, appams, duck curry. We haven't diluted original recipes. Our food is a flavour bomb; it is spicy by flavour, not by pungency."

— Regi Mathew, Chef and Co-founder, Chatti, New York

In Melbourne, Gujarati-origin chef Helly Raichura runs Enter Via Laundry, a 20-cover supper club with a waiting list of 9,000 people. Her appearance on MasterChef Australia in 2020, showcasing a playful take on the Gujarati staple khandvi, introduced global audiences to regional Indian cooking beyond the usual stereotypes.

Self-taught home cooks of Indian origin are also running supper clubs, pop-ups, and food festivals across the US, UK, and Australia, celebrating dishes from their ancestral towns and changing perceptions of Indian food as a homogeneous, heat-laden entity.

A Michelin Milestone

The shift is earning recognition at the highest levels of global gastronomy. Semma, a Michelin-starred South Indian restaurant in New York, was ranked No. 1 on The New York Times's 2025 list of the city's 100 best restaurants — the first Indian restaurant to top the list. Earlier, Chai Pani in North Carolina, which largely serves chaat, won the James Beard Foundation's Outstanding Restaurant award.

Award-winning chef Manish Mehrotra, who has been instrumental in elevating Indian cuisine through restaurants like Indian Accent, argues the movement needs to go beyond celebrity chefs. "The government must assist entrepreneurs in setting up authentic Indian restaurants across the globe," he said.

The Export Opportunity

The commercial stakes are significant. India's ready-to-eat and ready-to-cook exports grew to $1.69 billion in 2024-25, up from $1.52 billion the previous year. In the first five months of 2025-26, exports surged to $1.60 billion. Major destinations include the US, UK, UAE, Canada, Australia, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, and Germany.

"If India can standardize quality and build a strong global brand for its cuisine, it won't just boost exports — it will deepen cultural linkages and strengthen the country's soft-power footprint in a way that traditional diplomacy cannot."

— Dattesh Parulekar, Assistant Professor, International Relations, Goa University

The government also plans to participate in major international food festivals — Taste of London, the Melbourne Food and Wine Festival, the Dubai Food Festival, and the Singapore Food Festival — to popularize regional dishes and expand Indian cuisine's international reach. Officials are also working to help traders secure GI tags and patents for specialty food products.

Former NITI Aayog CEO Amitabh Kant has stressed the power of India-rooted chefs abroad. "Across the globe, countless Indian chefs have journeyed abroad and become culinary luminaries in their own right. India must harness this formidable resource by partnering with these chefs to promote Indian food through curated events and festivals," Kant wrote.
